title: Session 5 — Liabilities: Provisions, Bonds & Leases
summary: BBM140 Financial Reporting and Analysis — the definition of liabilities, provisions vs contingent liabilities (IAS 37), current vs non-current classification, present value, bonds (par, discount, zero-coupon) at amortised cost using the effective-interest method, and the accounting for leases.

blocks.title: 🎯 Learning objectives
items: Learn how to distinguish between provisions and contingent liabilities.
Discuss bond loans and their accounting treatment (amortised cost, effective interest).
Learn about lease contracts and their financial-reporting implications.

blocks.title: 1. What is a liability?
blocks.content:
Beside shareholders' equity, **liabilities** are the other source of funding for the business. Under GAAP a liability is:

1. a **present obligation** arising from **past events**;
2. a **probable future outflow** of resources from settling that obligation; and
3. an amount whose settlement can be **measured reliably**.

> If **one or more** of these criteria is **not** met, the item is a **contingent liability** (a loss contingency): it is **not recognised** on the balance sheet but is **disclosed** as an off-balance-sheet item.

blocks.title: 2. Contingent liabilities (off balance sheet)
blocks.content:
Examples that **cannot** be recognised on the balance sheet because they fail a criterion, but may need **disclosure**:

- A **commitment to purchase** non-current assets next year (unless there is a legally binding contract).
- A **remote but potential** liability for a defective product, where no court action has started.
- A **guarantee** supporting another company's bank overdraft, where there is very little likelihood of being called on.

The treatment turns on the **likelihood** of the future outflow: **probable** (likely to occur), **reasonably possible** (more than remote but less than likely), or **remote** (slight) — **and** whether the amount is **reasonably estimable**.

blocks.title: 3. Provisions (on the balance sheet) — IAS 37
blocks.content:
Sometimes the **existence** of an obligation is certain/highly likely but the **amount** is not. By **prudence**, when future expenditure is certain or highly likely but its **amount and/or timing is uncertain**, a **provision** is created — the **best estimate** of a future expected loss of resources. Recording a provision creates a **liability** in the B/S; the I/S counterpart is an **expense**.

**IAS 37** defines provisions as *liabilities of uncertain timing or amount*, recognised **when, and only when:**
- (a) the entity has a **present obligation** from a past event;
- (b) it is **probable** (more likely than not) that an outflow of resources will be required to settle it; and
- (c) a **reliable estimate** can be made of the amount.

**Types:** restructuring, environmental (e.g. remediation of past mining), decommissioning (e.g. dismantling an oil rig / nuclear plant), litigation and other legal claims.

blocks.title: 4. Provisions — worked examples
blocks.content:
**Alfa plc (2024).** A legal suit over compensation of former employees; legal advisors estimate a settlement of **£100,000**. Though not yet contractually obliged, **prudence** requires a provision for the best estimate. In **2025** the dispute settles for **£90,000**.

| | Cash | Provision | Profit (I/S) | Retained profit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2024 — recognise provision | | +100,000 | (100,000) | |
| 2024 — transfer to retained profit | | | +100,000 | (100,000) |
| 2025 — settle / cancel provision | (90,000) | (100,000) | +10,000 | |
| 2025 — transfer to retained profit | | | (10,000) | +10,000 |

The £100,000 provision is set up in 2024; on settlement for £90,000 the £10,000 over-provision is released back to profit in 2025.

**AstraZeneca (quick exercise).** AstraZeneca set aside **$4.5m** for a Chinese regulatory probe into suspected unpaid import taxes. If it later settles for **$4.4m**, it recognises a **provision of $4.5m** in the earlier quarter (I/S expense) and, on settlement, pays $4.4m and releases the $0.1m over-provision — exactly the Alfa pattern.

blocks.title: 5. Provision or contingency? — practice
blocks.content:
Classify each obligation as a **provision (recognise)**, a **contingent liability (disclose)**, or **no disclosure**:

- **Throughput / take-or-pay contracts** (e.g. Chevron pipeline; Alcoa gas & electricity) — pay even if the commodity/service is not used → typically a **contingency/commitment** disclosed (a present obligation may be a provision if a loss is probable and estimable).
- **Copyright infringement claim** where lawyers are confident of **winning** (Held Up Ltd) → outflow **not probable** → **contingency (disclose)**, no provision.
- **Warranty with a proven track record.** If experience shows warranties are **probable** to be used, make a **provision** (expected-value estimate); if returns have **never** occurred and are remote (Andox medical equipment) → **no provision** (possibly no disclosure).
- **Guarantee for a subsidiary in liquidation** where the company is **likely** to have to pay £500,000 → outflow **probable** and estimable → **provision**.

**Best-estimate examples:**
- **Legal claim £750,000, 30% chance of successfully defending** → 70% chance of losing (probable) → provide; best estimate ≈ the expected settlement (often the full £750,000, as it is a single most-likely outcome).
- **Warranty portfolio:** 80% no defects, 15% small defects (cost £5m), 5% major defects (cost £9m) → expected provision = 0.80×0 + 0.15×£5m + 0.05×£9m = **£1.20m** (0.75 + 0.45).

blocks.title: 6. Current vs non-current liabilities
blocks.content:
Liabilities are classified as **current** or **non-current (long-term)**.

**Current liabilities** — any of:
- expected to be **settled in the normal operating cycle**;
- held primarily **for trading**;
- **due within one year** of the balance-sheet date.

**Non-current liabilities** — if **none** of the above apply.

*Classify:* accounts payable → current; **bonds / long-term loans / mortgages** → non-current (unless due within a year); short-term borrowings → current; **current portion of long-term debt** → current; deposits, deferred revenues, capital leases, warranties → depends on timing.

**Measurement:**
- **Current liabilities** are reported at **nominal value**.
- **Non-current liabilities** are reported at **present value**, based on the interest rate when initiated.

blocks.title: 7. Present value (revision)
blocks.content:
Long-term liabilities are valued using **present value** — the value **today** of cash flows to be received/paid in future periods, reflecting the **time value of money**: £1 today is worth more than £1 in the future.

**Future value** of £1 today at rate r for one year: $FV = 1 \times (1+r)$. At 10%, £1 → £1.10.

**Present value** of a future cash flow $X$ received in $n$ periods at discount rate $r$:
$$PV = \frac{X}{(1+r)^n}$$

The factor $1/(1+r)^n$ is the **discount factor**, capturing interest rates, risk and opportunity cost.

**Examples (r = 10%):**
- £1,000 in **1 year**: $1{,}000 / 1.1 = £909.09$.
- £1,000 in **3 years**: $1{,}000 / 1.1^3 = £751.31$.

**Cash flows can only be added when at the same point in time (their PV).** Compare: (a) £1,000 in 3 years → PV £751.31 vs (b) £500 in 2 yrs + £500 in 3 yrs → $500/1.1^2 + 500/1.1^3 = £788.88$, so **(b) is preferred**.

**Exercise:** PV of a loan paying £3,000 (yr 1), £2,000 (yr 2), £1,500 (yr 3) at 5%:
$$\frac{3{,}000}{1.05} + \frac{2{,}000}{1.05^2} + \frac{1{,}500}{1.05^3} = £5{,}967$$

blocks.title: 8. Bonds — the basics
blocks.content:
A **bond** is a debt security: the **issuer (borrower)** owes the **bondholder (lender)** and must repay the **principal** and **interest (the coupon)** at/until **maturity**. Bonds are issued for a fixed term (usually **> 1 year**) to raise **large** amounts of financing.

- A bond issue is **costly** and usually needs a financial institution to arrange it and act as intermediary.
- It involves **many** bondholders (unknown to the company) — unlike a traditional loan with a single borrower and lender.

**Key terms:**
- **Face value (par / principal)** — the amount due at maturity.
- **Coupon rate** — the *stated* rate; **coupon payment = coupon rate × face value**.
- **Market (effective) interest rate** — the rate the market demands given the bond's risk; can be above or below the coupon rate.

**Price relative to face value:**

| Price | Condition |
|---|---|
| **At par** | stated rate = effective rate |
| **At a discount** (below par) | stated rate **<** effective rate |
| **At a premium** (above par) | stated rate **>** effective rate |

blocks.title: 9. Accounting for bonds — amortised cost & effective interest
blocks.content:
A bond liability (a held-to-maturity debt instrument) is recognised in the **B/S at amortised cost**; interest is recognised in the **I/S using the effective-interest method**.

$$\text{Amortised cost}_{\text{end}} = \text{Amortised cost}_{\text{begin}} + \text{Interest expense} - \text{Interest cash flow}$$

$$\text{Interest expense} = \text{Amortised cost}_{\text{begin}} \times \text{effective (market) rate}$$

The **cash interest paid** each period = **face value × coupon rate**. Any **difference** between interest expense and cash interest is **added to (or deducted from) the bond payable**, gradually amortising the discount/premium to face value by maturity.

blocks.title: 10. Bond issued at par
blocks.content:
**Example.** On 1 Jan X1 a company issues **£100** bonds (per £100 face) with a **9% annual coupon** paid at year-end; **market rate 9%**; principal repaid 31 Dec X2.

Since coupon = market rate, investors pay **face value**:
$$PV = \frac{9}{1.09} + \frac{109}{1.09^2} = £100$$

**At par, interest expense = cash interest = £9 each year**, so the bond payable stays at £100.

| | Cash | Bonds payable | Profit (I/S) | Retained profit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| X1 — bond issuance | +100 | +100 | | |
| X1 — interest expense | (9) | | (9) | |
| X1 — transfer to retained profit | | | +9 | (9) |
| **X1 closing** | **91** | **100** | | **(9)** |
| X2 — interest expense | (9) | | (9) | |
| X2 — principal repayment | (100) | (100) | | |
| X2 — transfer to retained profit | | | +9 | (9) |
| **X2 closing** | **(18)** | **0** | | **(18)** |

blocks.title: 11. Bond issued at a discount
blocks.content:
**Example.** Same £100 bond, **9% coupon**, but the market now requires **12%**. Investors will only pay the PV of the cash flows discounted at **12%**:
$$PV = \frac{9}{1.12} + \frac{109}{1.12^2} = £94.93$$

The firm receives **£94.93** (< face £100) because it is not offering the market rate. The **discount of £5.07** (= 100 − 94.93) is the PV of the interest 'shortfall'. On the B/S: Bond payable £100 *less* discount (£5.07) = **amortised cost (net bond payable) £94.93**.

**Amortisation schedule** (effective rate 12%):

| Period | Amortised cost (begin) | Interest expense = a×12% | Cash flow | Amortised cost (end) = a+b−c |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| X1 | 94.93 | 11.39 | 9 | 97.32 |
| X2 | 97.32 | 11.68 | 109 | 0 |

**Total interest expense** = 11.39 + 11.68 = **23.07**; **total cash paid** = 9 + 9 = 18; the difference **23.07 − 18 = 5.07** is the discount, recognised in the I/S over the bond's life (**matching**). Interest expense (based on amortised cost) **exceeds** the cash coupon each period, and the shortfall is added to the bond payable until it reaches face value at maturity.

| | Cash | Bonds payable | Profit (I/S) | Retained profit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| X1 — bond issuance | +94.93 | +94.93 | | |
| X1 — interest expense | (9) | +2.39 | (11.39) | |
| X1 closing | 85.93 | 97.32 | | (11.39) |
| X2 — interest expense | (9) | +2.68 | (11.68) | |
| X2 — principal repayment | (100) | (100) | | |
| **X2 closing** | **(23.07)** | **0** | | **(23.07)** |

blocks.title: 12. Zero-coupon bonds
blocks.content:
A **zero-coupon bond** pays **no cash interest** — only the nominal value at maturity. All the return comes from the **discount**.

**Example.** A zero-coupon bond paying **£1,000 in 3 years**, issued 31 Dec 2025; market rate **10%**.
$$PV = \frac{1{,}000}{1.10^3} = £751.31$$

At issue: receive cash £751.31; Bond payable £1,000 *less* discount £248.69 = amortised cost **£751.31**. Interest accrues each year (added to the bond payable) with **no cash flow** until maturity:

| Date | Amortised cost (begin) | Interest expense = a×10% | Cash flow | Amortised cost (end) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 31.12.2025 | 751.31 | 0 | 0 | 751.31 |
| 31.12.2026 | 751.31 | 75.13 | 0 | 826.44 |
| 31.12.2027 | 826.44 | 82.64 | 0 | 909.08 |
| 31.12.2028 | 909.08 | 90.92 | 1,000 | 0 |

Interest expense compounds on the growing amortised cost until it equals the £1,000 repaid at maturity.

blocks.title: 13. Leases — concept and rationale
blocks.content:
A **lease** is a contract between a **lessor** (legal owner of the asset) and a **lessee** (who rents it). The lessor keeps **legal ownership**; the lessee gets the **economic benefits** of the asset for an agreed period in exchange for rent. Examples: motor vehicles, aeroplanes, ships, machines, computer equipment.

**Operational advantages to the lessee:**
- **Flexibility** — avoid buying an asset needed only seasonally/temporarily; contracts can be tailored.
- **Protection against obsolescence** (e.g. computer equipment) — but payments are higher for it.
- **Ready-to-use** equipment is attractive when set-up would be lengthy.

**Financial advantages:**
- **Tax advantages** (in the UK, up to 100% relief on payments against tax).
- **Improves cash flow** — payments tailored to the lessee's cash flows; up to 100% financing; avoids large upfront cash / deposits.

**Disadvantages:** ready-to-use kit may be lower quality; high-quality kit may be unavailable to lease; seasonal leasing affects availability/prices; a premium is paid for obsolescence protection.

blocks.title: 14. Accounting for leases — finance vs operating
blocks.content:
**Finance (capital) lease** — if the agreement is for **more than 12 months**:
- the **lessee records the leased asset** in the B/S and the corresponding **lease obligation (liability)**;
- the I/S recognises **depreciation expense** (asset) **and interest expense** (liability, amortised).

**Operating lease** — if **not** a finance lease (short term):
- **no recognition** on the balance sheet;
- the lessee simply accrues **rent expense** in the I/S.

*(The lessor of a finance lease recognises it as a loan/receivable — the net investment ≈ the PV of the payments — and recognises finance income at a constant periodic rate of return.)*

blocks.title: 15. Finance lease — worked example
blocks.content:
**Example.** A non-cancellable 3-year lease with equal year-end rent of **£21,709**. Equipment fair value **£47,000**, useful life 4 years. The annual payment includes **£2,000** of property taxes (executory cost). Implicit interest rate **15%**; no renewal option; asset reverts to the lessor.

**Value the leased asset (PV of the debt component):**
$$PV = (21{,}709 - 2{,}000) \times 2.28323 = £45{,}000$$
where 2.28323 is the 3-year annuity factor at 15%. £45,000 is **95.7%** of fair value (£47,000), so it is a finance lease.

**Amortisation of the lease liability** (effective rate 15%; net rent 19,709):

| Period | Amortised cost (begin) | Interest = a×15% | Cash flow | Amortised cost (end) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 45,000 | 6,750 | 19,709 | 32,041 |
| 2 | 32,041 | 4,806 | 19,709 | 17,138 |
| 3 | 17,138 | 2,571 | 19,709 | 0 |

**Depreciation** = 45,000 (PV) ÷ 3 years (contract life) = **£15,000** p.a.

**Year 1 entries:** record asset & lease payable £45,000; depreciation (15,000); pay property tax (2,000) to the I/S; the £19,709 net payment splits into **interest £6,750 (I/S)** and **capital repayment £12,959** (reducing the lease payable to 32,041).

**Financial-reporting implications for the lessee:** the **asset and loan** appear on the B/S at inception; the **I/S** carries **interest + depreciation**; in the **cash-flow statement** the payment splits into interest (financing/operating outflow) and capital repayment (financing outflow).

items.definition: A present obligation from past events, with a probable future outflow of resources, measurable reliably. Fail a criterion and it becomes a contingent liability.
An obligation that fails a recognition criterion (e.g. outflow not probable, or not estimable); disclosed off balance sheet, not recognised.
A liability of uncertain timing or amount, recognised when there is a present obligation from a past event, a probable outflow, and a reliable estimate. Best estimate of a future loss.
Likelihood scale for future events: probable = likely; reasonably possible = more than remote but less than likely; remote = slight.
Current = settled in the operating cycle, held for trading, or due within one year; otherwise non-current. Current at nominal value, non-current at present value.
PV = X / (1+r)^n. Cash flows can only be added at the same point in time (their PVs).
A debt security obliging the issuer to pay coupons and repay principal at maturity; raises large financing from many investors.
Coupon (stated) rate sets the cash interest (coupon × face). Market rate is what investors demand; it sets the price.
Par: coupon = market rate. Discount: coupon < market rate (price below face). Premium: coupon > market rate (price above face).
Bond carried at amortised cost = opening + interest expense − cash interest; interest expense = opening amortised cost × effective rate.
Pays no cash interest; return is the discount. Interest accrues and compounds into the bond payable until it equals face value at maturity.
Finance lease (>12 months): asset + liability on the B/S, depreciation + interest in the I/S. Operating lease: off balance sheet, rent expense only.

blocks.title: 🧪 Try it yourself — present value, bond discount & lease amortisation
blocks.prompt: Reproduce the multi-cash-flow PV, price the 9%-coupon bond at a 12% market rate, and build the finance-lease amortisation schedule. Change the rates and cash flows to see par vs discount vs premium and how the schedules unwind to zero.
blocks.starter:
def pv(cfs, r):
    return sum(cf / (1 + r) ** (t + 1) for t, cf in enumerate(cfs))

# Multi-cash-flow loan PV at 5%
print(f"Loan PV @5% = {pv([3_000, 2_000, 1_500], 0.05):,.0f}")   # -> 5,967

# Price a 2-year 9%-coupon, 100-face bond at a 12% market rate
coupon, face, mkt = 9, 100, 0.12
price = pv([coupon, coupon + face], mkt)
print(f"Bond price @12% = {price:.2f}  (discount = {face - price:.2f})")

# Finance-lease liability amortisation: PV 45,000, rate 15%, net rent 19,709
bal, rate, rent = 45_000, 0.15, 19_709
for yr in range(1, 4):
    interest = round(bal * rate)
    bal = bal + interest - rent
    print(f"Year {yr}: interest={interest:>6,}  closing balance={bal:>7,}")

cards.back: Present obligation from a past event; probable future outflow of resources; amount measurable reliably. Fail one → contingent liability.
Provision = probable + estimable → recognised (IAS 37). Contingent = fails a criterion (e.g. only possible) → disclosed off balance sheet.

cards.front: Warranty provision: 80% none, 15% small (£5m), 5% major (£9m). Best estimate?
How are current vs non-current liabilities measured?
cards.back: Current at nominal value; non-current at present value (rate at initiation).
PV = X / (1+r)^n. Only add cash flows once they are at the same date (their PVs).
Par: coupon = market rate. Discount: coupon < market. Premium: coupon > market.

cards.front: Interest expense under the effective-interest method?
cards.back: Opening amortised cost × effective (market) rate. Cash interest = coupon × face; the difference adjusts the bond payable.

cards.front: How does a zero-coupon bond's liability behave?
cards.back: Starts at PV, accrues compounding interest (no cash) each year, and reaches face value at maturity.
Finance (>12m): asset + liability on B/S, depreciation + interest in I/S. Operating: off B/S, only rent expense.

questions.q: A company is likely (probable) to lose a lawsuit and can estimate the amount reliably. How is this treated?
options: Disclosed as a contingent liability only
Recognised as a provision (liability + I/S expense)
questions.explanation: Present obligation + probable outflow + reliable estimate → IAS 37 requires a provision, with an expense in the I/S.

questions.q: Warranty experience: 80% no defect, 15% small defect costing £5m, 5% major costing £9m. Best-estimate provision?
A £100-face bond has a 9% coupon, but the market demands 12%. The bond will be issued:
questions.explanation: Coupon (9%) < market rate (12%), so investors pay less than face: PV at 12% ≈ £94.93 — a discount.

questions.q: Under the effective-interest method, a discounted bond's interest expense compared with the cash coupon is:
options: Always equal to the cash coupon
Higher than the cash coupon, with the difference added to the bond payable
questions.explanation: Interest expense = amortised cost × effective rate, which exceeds the cash coupon; the shortfall increases the bond payable toward face value.

questions.q: A zero-coupon bond pays £1,000 in 3 years; market rate 10%. Its issue price is:
questions.explanation: PV = 1,000 / 1.10³ = £751.31. The £248.69 difference is the discount amortised to maturity.

questions.q: A non-cancellable lease runs for 3 years (>12 months). For the lessee, this is:
options: An operating lease — only rent expense
A finance lease — asset and liability on the B/S, with depreciation and interest
questions.explanation: A lease for more than 12 months is a finance lease: the lessee capitalises the asset and lease liability and recognises depreciation plus interest.

blocks.title: 📝 Recap
blocks.content: Liabilities are present obligations from past events with a probable, reliably measurable outflow; fail a criterion and the item is a contingent liability that is only disclosed. Provisions (IAS 37) recognise obligations that are probable and estimable but uncertain in timing/amount, at best estimate (e.g. expected-value warranty provisions). Liabilities split into current (nominal value) and non-current (present value), and present value discounts future cash flows at PV = X/(1+r)^n. Bonds are carried at amortised cost with interest recognised on the effective-interest method: issued at par (coupon = market), at a discount (coupon < market) or premium (coupon > market), with zero-coupon bonds accruing all return as compounding discount. Finance leases (>12 months) put the asset and lease liability on the lessee's balance sheet with depreciation and interest in the I/S, while operating leases stay off balance sheet as rent expense.
